title: Fast Powers mod n
short: Square again and again, multiply the powers that match the binary digits of the exponent, and reduce after every step.
trouble: Students compute the whole power before reducing, which makes the numbers far too large. Reduce after every multiplication.

blocks.html: Cryptography constantly needs numbers like $a^{e} \bmod n$ with exponents hundreds of digits long. Multiplying $a$ by itself $e$ times would take longer than the age of the universe. Two ideas make it instant: reduce mod $n$ after every multiplication (allowed by modular arithmetic), and build the exponent from its binary digits.

items: Write $e$ in binary, that is, as a sum of powers of 2.
Square again and again: $a^{1}, a^{2}, a^{4}, a^{8}, \dots$, each one the square of the one before, reduced mod $n$.
Multiply together the powers whose binary digit is 1, reducing after each multiplication.

blocks.html: Since $a^{s + t} = a^{s} a^{t}$, a sum of powers of two in the exponent becomes a product of the squares you computed. Each square is the square of the previous one, so reaching $a^{2^{k}}$ takes only $k$ squarings. An exponent with $k + 1$ binary digits needs at most $k$ squarings and $k$ more multiplications: for a 600-digit exponent, about 4,000 steps instead of $10^{600}$. Reducing each time keeps every number below $n^{2}$.

Count the work: three squarings and two multiplications, five in all, instead of the twelve multiplications of $5 \cdot 5 \cdots 5$. And no number above $22^{2} = 484$ ever appeared. (Check by brute force: $5^{13} = 1{,}220{,}703{,}125 = 23 \cdot 53{,}074{,}048 + 21$.)

blocks.name: nt-powers
blocks.cap: The table for $3^{45} \bmod 100$, the last two digits of $3^{45}$: one row per binary digit of 45, the repeated squares, and the running product of the rows whose bit is 1. Change the exponent and watch how few rows it needs.

blocks.title: Last two digits
blocks.q: Find the last two digits of $3^{45}$.

blocks.html: Computing the whole power first. $3^{45} = 2{,}954{,}312{,}706{,}550{,}833{,}698{,}643$ already has 22 digits, and a calculator rounds it, so its last digits come out wrong. Reduce after every multiplication, so no number ever exceeds $(n - 1)^{2}$. And do not reduce the exponent mod $n$: $3^{45} \not\equiv 3^{45 \bmod 100}$ in general. (The right way to shrink exponents comes with Fermat's theorem.)
Write the exponent in binary, square repeatedly, multiply the squares you need, and reduce mod $n$ after every multiplication. About $2\log_2 e$ multiplications suffice.
